core_idea: Classify each game state by the minimum 2-adic valuation (the position of the least significant set bit) among piles. Its parity, together with whether every pile attains that minimum, determines a forced win, loss, or indefinitely maintainable draw; then count initial arrays by their exact minimum valuation.
key_observations: The move rule is governed by divisibility by powers of two, so full pile values can be compressed to their least-significant-set-bit positions.
If every pile has the same positive valuation c, any move makes every valuation exactly c-1.
When the minimum valuation is odd, moving a pile at that minimum synchronizes all piles at the next lower, even valuation, creating a losing state for the opponent.
When the minimum valuation is even and shared by all piles, every possible move gives the opponent the corresponding odd-minimum winning state.

When an even minimum is not shared by all piles, a player can move a pile strictly above the minimum while preserving both a minimum-level pile and a higher-level pile; this prevents termination forever.
Arrays with exact minimum valuation i can be counted by subtracting arrays whose valuations are all at least i+1 from those whose valuations are all at least i.
The losing-player configurations require a stricter condition than a fixed minimum: every element must have exactly the same even valuation.
reasoning_patterns: Reduce numerical game states to the smallest valuation or other operation-relevant invariant.
Classify impartial-game positions using a compact state signature and parity.
Use a synchronizing move that collapses many components to a uniform next state.
Prove draws by exhibiting a closed set of nonterminal states that each player can preserve.
Count objects by exact minimum via the difference of two cumulative counts.
Separate a special uniform case from the general minimum-based classification.
questions: What divisibility information does every move actually depend on?
Can the state be compressed to a valuation or minimum invariant?
What happens if all components share the same critical value?
Can I move at the minimum to force a canonical next state?
Is there a nonterminal state family that both players can preserve forever?
Can configurations with an exact minimum be counted by subtracting cumulative cases?
